newsitem.title: GERMANY: Waigel's semantics seen irrelevant for EMU outcome.
newsitem.headline: Waigel's semantics seen irrelevant for EMU outcome.

text.p: German Finance Minister Theo Waigel retreated to his rigid stance on EMU at the weekend but analysts said the step was politically-motivated and would have little relevance in the final countdown to the single currency.

"Waigel has come full circle now, but as long as the political will remains for Germany to join EMU, then the project would not collapse because of this view," said Stefan Schneider, economist at Banque Paribas in Frankfurt.

At issue was Waigel's view on the requirement that European Union member nations must report 1997 budget deficits of no more than three percent of gross domestic product to join the currency union at its planned 1999 launch date.

Insisting he had not softened his stance on EMU, Waigel nonetheless spent most of last week either avoiding numbers completely or speaking only of "three percent" not "3.0 percent" as he had done only several months earlier.

But at a weekend party meeting of his ultra-conservative Christian Social Union, Waigel agreed with a party motion that "three" should mean "3.0 percent", insisting "I have said the goal is to be three and not three plus x".

The quibbling over exactly what "three" means has become a central point of political debate about EMU in Germany as high unemployment and fragile growth place a question mark over Bonn's ability to meet its 1997 deficit goal of 2.9 percent.

Economists saw last week's "Waigel waffle" as an ill-fated attempt to appease a more moderate faction of Helmut Kohl's Christian Democrats, after some members had linked painful austerity measures to the currency project.

"It sounds plausible that Waigel was forced into 3.0 percent by Stoiber," said Merrill Lynch economist Joerg Kraemer referring to a bitter power struggle between Waigel, the head of the party and Stoiber, the premier of Bavaria.
"Waigel could not appear as a softie at that party meeting," Paribas' Schneider added.
While the return to hardline rhetoric may complicate Waigel's life, economists agreed the position could have benefits, like keeping up pressure on German budget savings.

And economists said the tough stance might even calm a German public, reluctant to give up the mark, by optically raising chances that southern nations, like Italy and Spain, can be kept out of the union.
Markets too were finding more pleasure in German officials' never-tiring insistence that the entry criteria would be met strictly, than last week's semantics on "three or 3.0 percent".
"The markets are basically concentrating on how this situation affects the chance for the southern states to get in," Merrill's Kraemer said.
Ultimately economists agreed there was plenty of time for Waigel to shift his position and speculated he might do so when more economic data is known.

Presenting reams of data ranging from March's 11.7 percent jobless rate to higher government net borrowing, economists said it was more likely Germany's 1997 budget deficit would be near 3.2 percent, not at Waigel's 2.9 percent goal.

"I think Waigel will stick to the official line until he absolutely can not avoid the facts any longer and becomes really obvious Germany will miss the criteria. But right now there are still so many uncertainties, so why should he give up already," Kraemer said.
Schneider argued a shift now would only mean that Waigel was giving up an important bargaining chip, to keep certain nations out, prematurely.
"Waigel will keep this up as long as he can, and in the end when Kohl takes him aside and says 3.2 is okay too, it will be okay and Germany will be in."
